per_question.question: What are the entrance, continued service, and discharge criteria for outpatient behavioral health services in NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid’s outpatient behavioral health policy sets the criteria as follows:

## Entrance criteria
A beneficiary must meet these criteria:
- Have a current **DSM-5 diagnosis**;
- Present with **behavioral, psychological, or biological dysfunction and functional impairment** consistent with and associated with that diagnosis;
- If a higher level of care is indicated but unavailable, or the beneficiary refuses it, outpatient services may be used **until the higher level of care is available** or to support the beneficiary’s participation in that higher level of care;
- Be **capable of developing skills** to manage symptoms, make behavioral changes, and respond favorably to treatment; and
- Have **no evidence that alternative interventions would be more effective** under North Carolina community practice standards.  
Cite: § 3.2.1.1, [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment) (effective Apr. 15, 2025; current authoritative document).

## Continued service criteria
Continued outpatient behavioral health services require:

### First, at least one of these:
- The desired outcome or level of functioning **has not been restored, improved, or sustained** within the timeframe in the treatment plan;
- The beneficiary **continues to be at risk for relapse** based on current clinical assessment and history; or
- The beneficiary’s functional gains are **tenuous**.

### And, in addition, at least one of these:
- The beneficiary has achieved current treatment plan goals, but **additional goals are indicated** by documented symptoms; or
- The beneficiary is **making satisfactory progress** toward meeting goals, with supporting documentation.  
Cite: § 3.2.1.2, [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment) (effective Apr. 15, 2025; current authoritative document).

## Discharge criteria
Discharge is appropriate when:
- The beneficiary’s **level of functioning has improved** in relation to treatment plan goals;
- The beneficiary or legally responsible person **no longer wants the services**; or
- The beneficiary has **not improved despite treatment plan modifications** and needs a more appropriate best practice or evidence-based treatment modality under North Carolina community practice standards.  
Cite: § 3.2.1.3, [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment) (effective Apr. 15, 2025; current authoritative document).

## Documentation note
The policy also requires the record to include **documentation of entrance criteria, continued service criteria, and discharge criteria**. Cite: § 7.3.1, [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment).

If you want, I can also turn this into a short attorney/case-manager checklist for chart review or medical-necessity appeals.

per_question.question: How does the EPSDT special provision affect coverage for outpatient therapy services, and what ordering practitioner requirements apply to beneficiaries under 21?
per_question.agent_answer:
For beneficiaries under 21, the **EPSDT special provision can expand coverage for outpatient therapy services beyond ordinary policy limits when the service is medically necessary to correct or ameliorate a defect, physical or mental illness, or condition**. But **EPSDT does not waive prior approval requirements**: if the therapy service requires prior approval, the child’s age does not eliminate that requirement. Also, the policy still excludes services that are **unsafe, ineffective, experimental/investigational, not medical in nature, or not generally recognized as accepted medical practice**. [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment) § 2.2.1; [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), “EPSDT and Prior Approval Requirements” (effective 2025-02-01; current, no amendments returned).

## What that means for outpatient therapy coverage

- **Baseline rule:** outpatient specialized therapies must still be **medically necessary** under Policy 10A.
- **EPSDT effect for under-21 beneficiaries:** Medicaid may cover a service for a beneficiary under 21 even if it exceeds a usual policy limitation, so long as it fits EPSDT’s medical-necessity standard and is not otherwise excluded as unsafe, ineffective, experimental/investigational, or non-medical. [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment) § 2.2.1.
- **Prior approval still applies:** Policy 10A expressly says that for services requiring prior approval, **being under 21 does not remove that requirement**. [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), “EPSDT and Prior Approval Requirements.”
- For pediatric speech-language and audiology therapy, Policy 10A also gives **under-21 medical-necessity visit guidelines** tied to severity, with authorization periods not exceeding six calendar months in the cited pediatric therapy section. [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment) § 5.4.

## Ordering practitioner requirements

Policy 10A’s listed **ordering practitioners** are:

- Medical Doctor (MD)
- Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine (DO)
- Doctor of Podiatric Medicine (DPM)
- Certified Nurse Midwife (CNM)
- Physician Assistant (PA)
- Nurse Practitioner (NP)

[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment) § 3.1.2 (effective 2025-02-01; current, no amendments returned).

## Under-21 documentation/discipline-specific points

For beneficiaries under 21, the therapy sections in Policy 10A add pediatric criteria and documentation standards, including severity-based and deficit-based criteria for services such as:

- **Speech-language therapy**: requires documented findings supporting dysphagia-related deficits or other qualifying pediatric impairment criteria described in the section. [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment) § 3.2.1.3.
- **Audiology therapy (aural rehabilitation)**: requires documented hearing-loss or auditory-processing findings and measurable functional limitations. [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment) § 3.2.1.4.

One caution: I could verify the list of authorized **ordering practitioner types** in § 3.1.2, but I did **not** find separate text in the retrieved sections imposing a different ordering-practitioner category specifically for beneficiaries under 21. So based on the text I could verify, the same listed practitioner categories apply, while under-21 beneficiaries may benefit from EPSDT-expanded coverage if medical necessity is established and prior approval rules are followed.

per_question.question: Does NC Medicaid cover Personal Care Services for beneficiaries who live in an assisted living facility?

Under NC Medicaid’s congregate PCS policy, coverage applies when the beneficiary resides in a congregate facility licensed by North Carolina as an Adult Care Home or certain licensed group homes, and otherwise meets the functional and medical criteria for PCS. The policy’s assessment rules also specifically contemplate assessments being done in the beneficiary’s congregate facility. - Coverage is not automatic just because the person lives in assisted living.
- The beneficiary must meet the PCS need standard in § 3.2.1, including qualifying ADL limitations and the other listed conditions.
- PCS is not covered if the beneficiary does not meet Section 3.0 criteria generally. See [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment), § 4.1.
- PCS in this policy is also not covered if it is provided somewhere other than the beneficiary’s primary congregate living setting, among other additional exclusions. See [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment), § 4.2.1.

So the short answer is: yes, NC Medicaid does cover PCS in assisted-living-type congregate settings, but only for beneficiaries in qualifying licensed settings who satisfy the policy’s eligibility requirements. per_question.question: Can a CAP/DA beneficiary transfer between service providers, and what rules govern transfers of eligible beneficiaries?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes. A CAP/DA beneficiary can transfer, and the CAP/DA policy sets specific coordination rules to govern that transfer. Under current CAP/DA policy, the case management entity must coordinate the transfer so there are no gaps in services. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) (effective Sept. 1, 2025, current per amendment check), § 3.3.

## Rules governing transfers of eligible beneficiaries

### General transfer requirements
Before a transfer occurs, the CME must complete these steps:

- determine the anticipated service start date;
- coordinate a transition plan between provider agencies;
- discuss and plan for the beneficiary’s health, safety, and well-being;
- initiate transfer of the electronic health record in the CAP Business System (e-CAP/DA) to the receiving county;
- arrange a home visit within five business days after the beneficiary moves to the new primary residence, so the receiving entity can assess the home environment and identify health and welfare concerns; and
- coordinate services so they begin on the first date of the transfer.  
  [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment), § 3.3.

### If the beneficiary is transferring to a different county
For a CAP/DA beneficiary moving from one county to another, the policy is more specific:

- the transferring CME and receiving CME must coordinate the transfer on the agreed transfer date, or in less than 30 calendar days from the request to transfer;
- both agencies must discuss and plan for the beneficiary’s health, safety, and well-being;
- the electronic health record must be transferred to the receiving county;
- the receiving CME must arrange a home visit within five business days after the move to assess the new residence and identify health and welfare concerns; and
- services must start on the first day of the transfer into the receiving county.  
  [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment), § 3.3.

## Related beneficiary choice and provider rules
The CAP/DA service plan must reflect the beneficiary’s right to choose among Medicaid-enrolled providers, documented with a signed Freedom of Choice form. That supports the conclusion that beneficiaries are not locked into one provider and may choose another provider, subject to the transfer procedures above. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment), § 5.4.2.

Also, covered CAP/DA services must be provided according to the approved service plan and applicable federal and state requirements. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment), § 3.2.1.

## Federal authority
I could not verify from the retrieved text that 42 CFR Part 413 governs beneficiary transfers in CAP/DA. The section identified in the frame, 42 CFR 413.64, addresses provider payment rules rather than transfer rights or transfer procedures. [42 CFR Part 413](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-413), § 413.64.

## Bottom line
A CAP/DA beneficiary may transfer between providers or counties, but the transfer must be coordinated by the involved CMEs to avoid any interruption in services, protect the beneficiary’s health and safety, transfer the record, complete a timely home visit, and ensure services begin on the effective transfer date. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment), § 3.3.

per_question.question: Is there a maximum earned income limit for people on HCWD (Health Coverage for Workers with Disabilities), and what premiums apply?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes—HCWD does **not** have a maximum **earned** income limit in the materials I could verify. But it **does** have:
- an **unearned income cap** of **more than 150% of FPL = not eligible**, and
- **cost-sharing** that increases with total countable income. [[MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)] [[CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 01-14, HCWD Phase III](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma_cn01-14.pdf)]

## Income limit

The governing HCWD eligibility section says the person must “meet the income requirements for his coverage group,” but the more specific income section states:

- “Those who have **unearned incomes greater than 150% of FPL are not eligible for HCWD**.” [[MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)]
- The HCWD Phase III change notice says MA-2180 was revised “to **remove limits on countable income except for the 150% of Federal Poverty Level (FPL) cap on unearned income** and provide information about sliding scale premiums.” [[CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 01-14, HCWD Phase III](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma_cn01-14.pdf)]

So based on the verified text, there is **no maximum earned income limit** stated for HCWD. The clear eligibility cap is on **unearned income**, not earned income. [[MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)] [[CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 01-14, HCWD Phase III](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma_cn01-14.pdf)]

## Premiums and fees

The verified HCWD policy says:

- If **total countable income is 150% of FPL or less**: **no cost sharing** other than applicable copayments. [[MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)]
- If **total countable income is greater than 150% of FPL**: the person must pay a **$50 annual enrollment fee**. [[MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)]

[[MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)]

I also verified that **MA-2180 has later amendments**, including **CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 03-25, 2025 Federal Poverty Level Changes (FPL) Income Changes**, whose change summary says: “**MA-2180.IV.I - HCWD Premiums Income chart has been updated**.” [[CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 03-25, 2025 Federal Poverty Level Changes (FPL) Income Changes](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/CN-NO-03-25.docx.pdf)]

## Bottom line

per_question.question: What is the federal statutory authority for NC's CAP/DA waiver, and what does the state need to demonstrate in its waiver application?
per_question.agent_answer:
**Federal authority:** NC’s CAP/DA waiver is a **Medicaid home- and community-based services waiver under section 1915(c) of the Social Security Act**, as implemented through **42 C.F.R. Part 441, Subpart G**. The federal rule governing what a waiver request must contain is **42 C.F.R. § 441.301**, which expressly refers to “the State’s **1915(c) HCBS waiver**.” [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

## What the state must demonstrate in its waiver application

Under **42 C.F.R. § 441.301**, the state’s waiver request must include, at minimum:

- **Required assurances and supporting documentation** required by §§ 441.302 and 441.303. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)
- **Any requested waivers of Medicaid state plan requirements**, when applicable, including:
  - statewide applicability,
  - comparability of services, and
  - certain income/resource rules for medically needy individuals in the community. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)
- A statement whether the state will deny HCBS when it reasonably expects the cost to exceed the cost of equivalent institutional care in a hospital, nursing facility, or ICF/IID. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

If the state is furnishing HCBS under the waiver, the request must also show that:

per_question.question: How many days of therapeutic leave from a nursing facility does NC Medicaid allow per year, and what conditions must be met?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid allows **up to 60 days of therapeutic leave per calendar year** for a Medicaid-eligible resident whose nursing facility bed is being reimbursed by Medicaid. No more than **15 consecutive therapeutic leave days** may be taken **without NC Medicaid approval**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8, effective 2024-08-07; current per amendment check]

## Conditions that must be met
Therapeutic leave must meet all of these conditions:

- It must be **for therapeutic purposes only**.
- It must be **ordered by the resident’s attending physician**.
- The **need for the leave must be documented in the resident’s plan of care**.
- A **therapeutic justification for each instance** of leave must be entered in the resident’s **health record**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8]

## Other important limits
- The facility must **reserve the resident’s bed** during the leave.
- The facility may not receive any other Medicaid revenue for that resident during the absence besides the **bed reimbursement**.
- The facility is reimbursed at its **full current Medicaid bed rate** for the reserved bed.
- Medicaid does **not** reimburse therapeutic leave days that **exceed the legal limit**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8]

## When therapeutic leave does not apply
Therapeutic leave entitlement **does not apply** if the resident is away **to receive inpatient or nursing services** somewhere else, or at a **different level of care in the same facility**, when those services are **paid by Medicaid**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8]

## Recordkeeping / review
- The therapeutic justification is subject to **State review**.
- Facilities must keep a **cumulative record** of leave days for each resident.
- Residents on therapeutic leave must be identified on the facility’s **midnight census**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8]

If you want, I can also give you a one-paragraph version you can cite in an appeal or facility dispute.

per_question.question: If a Private Duty Nursing provider terminates services for a Medicaid beneficiary, what notification requirements must they follow?
per_question.agent_answer:
A PDN provider that discharges a Medicaid beneficiary must notify **NC Medicaid**, and the required notice depends on why services are ending.

## NC Medicaid PDN policy requirements

Under **Section 5.2.4.1, “Notification of Termination,”** of **[3G-1 Private Duty Nursing for Beneficiaries Age 21 and Older](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment)**, the provider must:

- **If the PDN provider discharges the beneficiary:**  
  submit the **DMA-3513 (PDN Discharge Summary Form)** to **NC Medicaid within 5 business days**.

- **If the provider discharges the beneficiary because another source of nursing coverage exists:**  
  **notify NC Medicaid** and submit the **DMA-3513 within 5 business days**. The notice must include:
  - the **last date PDN services were provided and billable to Medicaid**, and
  - the **name of the other source of coverage**.

- **If the attending physician discharges the beneficiary:**  
  the PDN provider must send NC Medicaid, **within 5 business days**:
  - the **attending physician’s order terminating PDN services**, and
  - the **DMA-3513**.

- **If services end because the beneficiary loses NC Medicaid eligibility, or no PDN services are provided for 30 consecutive days (including hospitalization):**  
  the policy says the **prior approval process must be started again** under Sections 5.1 and 5.2 before PDN resumes.  
  Citation: **Section 5.2.4.1** of **[3G-1 Private Duty Nursing for Beneficiaries Age 21 and Older](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment)**. I checked amendments for this document, and the tool returned **3G-1 as the authoritative current document**.

## Beneficiary notice / appeal rights

The NC PDN policy draws an important distinction:

- If the **attending physician and/or the PDN provider** discharges the beneficiary, that decision **cannot be appealed to NC Medicaid** under Section 5.2.4.1.
- But if **NC Medicaid** terminates PDN because review shows Medicaid eligibility, policy criteria, or medical necessity is not met, **NC Medicaid or its designee must give written notice to the beneficiary/legal representative that includes appeal rights**.  
  Citation: **Section 5.2.4.1** of **[3G-1 Private Duty Nursing for Beneficiaries Age 21 and Older](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment)**.

## If the beneficiary is in managed care

If the termination is being made by an **MCO/PIHP/PAHP** as an adverse benefit determination, federal managed-care rules require **timely and adequate written notice** to the enrollee, consistent with **[42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)**:

- the notice must be **in writing**,
- explain the action and reasons,
- explain appeal rights and fair hearing rights,
- explain how to request expedited review, and
- explain continuation-of-benefits rights where applicable.  
  See **42 C.F.R. § 438.404** and the accessibility/language requirements in **42 C.F.R. § 438.10**. I checked amendments for **[42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)**, and the tool returned it as the **authoritative current document**.

## Bottom line

For a PDN provider termination under NC Medicaid PDN policy, the core rule is:

- **Notify NC Medicaid within 5 business days**, and
- submit the **DMA-3513 PDN Discharge Summary Form**,
- with extra information if another coverage source is replacing Medicaid PDN,
- and include the physician’s termination order if the physician initiated discharge.

If you want, I can also pull the exact rule for **reduction** of PDN hours/services, which is separate from termination.

per_question.question: What does federal law define as 'home health services' under Medicaid, and where must they be provided?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under federal Medicaid law, **“home health services”** are the services listed in **42 C.F.R. § 440.70(b)** when they are provided **at the beneficiary’s place of residence** and under the required practitioner orders and plan-of-care rules. Those services include:

- **Nursing services** provided on a part-time or intermittent basis,
- **Home health aide services,**
- **Medical supplies, equipment, and appliances** suitable for use in normal-life settings, and
- **Physical therapy, occupational therapy, or speech pathology and audiology services** (this therapy category is optional for states, while the first three categories are required home health benefit components). [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

## Federal rule

Under **42 C.F.R. § 440.70(a)-(b)**, home health services must be:

- provided **at the beneficiary’s place of residence**;
- furnished on **orders written by a physician, nurse practitioner, clinical nurse specialist, or physician assistant** working in accordance with state law for the services described in § 440.70(b)(1), (2), and (4);
- included in a **written plan of care**; and
- that plan of care must be **reviewed by the ordering practitioner every 60 days** for those services.

For **medical supplies, equipment, and appliances** under § 440.70(b)(3), the rule separately requires physician or other licensed practitioner orders under state-law scope-of-practice rules and a written plan of care, with review as specified in that subsection. [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

## Where they must be provided

Federal law says home health services must be provided at the beneficiary’s **“place of residence.”** But the regulation also says what **does not** count as a place of residence for this purpose.

Under **42 C.F.R. § 440.70(c)**, a beneficiary’s place of residence **does not include**:

- a **hospital**,
- a **nursing facility**, or
- an **intermediate care facility for individuals with intellectual disabilities (ICF/IID)**,

**except** that certain home health services may be provided in an **ICF/IID** if those services are **not required to be provided by the facility** itself. [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

The rule further states that nothing in § 440.70 allows states to restrict home health only to traditional in-home settings. A beneficiary may receive home health services in **“any setting in which normal life activities take place,”** other than:

- a hospital,
- a nursing facility,
- an ICF/IID, or
- **any setting where Medicaid payment is or could be made for inpatient services that include room and board.**

The regulation also explicitly says **home health services cannot be limited to beneficiaries who are homebound**. [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

## Supporting context

A separate federal home- and community-based services provision, **42 C.F.R. § 440.182**, includes **home health aide services** as one possible HCBS benefit category, but that is a different state-plan benefit structure from the core home health definition in **§ 440.70**. So the governing federal definition for your question is **§ 440.70**, not the HCBS section. [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

## Bottom line

Federal Medicaid law defines **home health services** as specified nursing, aide, medical-supply/equipment/appliance, and certain therapy services provided under required orders and a written plan of care. They must be furnished at the beneficiary’s **place of residence**, which can include **settings where normal life activities take place**, but **not** a **hospital**, **nursing facility**, or generally an **ICF/IID**, and not any setting paid as inpatient room-and-board care. [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

per_question.question: How does NC Medicaid define 'terminally ill' for purposes of hospice eligibility, and what certification is required?
per_question.agent_answer:
For NC Medicaid hospice, **“terminally ill” means the beneficiary has a life expectancy of six months or less**. The policy text reflects this standard in the certification requirements, including for later recertifications, which must explain why the clinical findings support **“a life expectancy of six months or less.”** [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment) (effective Mar. 15, 2024), section “D. Certification and Recertification of Terminal Illness”; see also § 5.4.1.

## Required certification

NC Medicaid requires **written certification of terminal illness for each benefit period**. The hospice provider must obtain the written certification **before submitting a claim for payment**. If the written certification cannot be obtained within two calendar days after a benefit period begins, an **oral certification must be obtained within two calendar days**, and the written certification must still be obtained before the claim is submitted. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment), § 5.4.1.

### Who must sign it
- **Initial 90-day period:** certification must come from  
  - the **medical director of the hospice** or the **physician member of the hospice interdisciplinary group (IDG)**; and  
  - the beneficiary’s **attending physician**, if the beneficiary has one.  
- **Subsequent periods:** only the **medical director of the hospice** or the **physician member of the hospice IDG** is required.  
[Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment), § 5.4.3.

### What the certification must contain
The certification or recertification must include:
- a physician narrative briefly synthesizing the clinical information supporting the terminal diagnosis;
- the physician’s attestation that the narrative was composed after reviewing the clinical information and, where applicable, examining the beneficiary;
- content reflecting the beneficiary’s **individual clinical circumstances**;
- the **election period dates** to which the certification applies; and
- the certifying or recertifying physician’s **signature and date**.  
For the **third and later election periods**, the narrative must also explain why the clinical findings from the required face-to-face encounter support a life expectancy of six months or less. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment), section “D. Certification and Recertification of Terminal Illness.”

### Timing details
- Initial certifications may be completed **no more than 15 calendar days before** the effective date of election.
- Recertifications may be completed **no more than 15 calendar days before** the start of the next benefit period.
- Before the **3rd benefit period recertification and every recertification after that**, a hospice physician or hospice nurse practitioner must have a **face-to-face encounter** with the beneficiary, occurring prior to, but no more than **30 calendar days before**, the recertification. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment), § 5.4.1; section “D. Certification and Recertification of Terminal Illness.”

I checked amendments for Policy 3D and found no listed amendments in the corpus; the authoritative document returned was **Hospice Services, effective March 15, 2024**.

per_question.question: What ambulance services are NOT covered by NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid does **not** cover certain ambulance services and charges, including these item-specific exclusions:

- when an ambulance is called and **no treatment is needed**
- when the ambulance responds to a **false alarm**
- when the beneficiary **refuses all medical services**
- when the ambulance transport is for a **medical service that is not a Medicaid-covered service**
- **commercial airline tickets**
- **airstrip fees**
- **taxes** charged separately (local, state, federal, etc.)
- **separate additional charges for nursing personnel** who are employees of a facility or ambulance service
- **waiting fees**
- **separate charges for oxygen, items, and supplies**, because those are included in the base rate
- **services other than those listed in Subsection 3.2** of the policy ([Ambulance Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment), § 4.2.1.4, effective 12/15/2023).

NC Medicaid also does **not** reimburse loaded mileage to a facility that is **not the nearest appropriate facility**. The beneficiary’s preference, or whether a physician has staff privileges at a particular hospital, does not determine whether the farther facility is appropriate ([Ambulance Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment), § 4.2.1).

More generally, ambulance services are not covered if:

- the beneficiary does not meet the **eligibility requirements** in Section 2.0
- the beneficiary does not meet the **coverage criteria** in Section 3.0
- the service **duplicates another provider’s service**
- the service is **experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial** ([Ambulance Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment), § 4.1).

The current authoritative policy I relied on is **Clinical Coverage Policy 15, Ambulance Services**, effective **December 15, 2023** ([Ambulance Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)).

per_question.question: Under what conditions can speech therapy be provided via telehealth under NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes—NC Medicaid allows some speech-language evaluation and treatment services to be provided by telehealth, but only under specific conditions.

## When speech therapy can be provided by telehealth

Under **Clinical Coverage Policy 10A**, a select set of speech and language evaluation and treatment interventions may be delivered by telehealth. Telehealth may be **medically necessary** when:

- the beneficiary’s medical condition means **exposure to others should be avoided**; or
- the beneficiary is in a **remote or underserved location** where access to appropriately qualified providers is limited.  
  [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), effective Feb. 1, 2025]

## Required limits on telehealth use

NC Medicaid says telehealth speech therapy must also meet these beneficiary-focused conditions:

- **It must be used as an adjunct to in-person care, not a replacement**, unless in-person care is contraindicated or unavailable.
- **It must be in the beneficiary’s best interest**, not for the therapist’s convenience.
- **It cannot be used solely to increase therapist productivity.**  
  [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), “e. Telehealth,” effective Feb. 1, 2025; current document confirmed]

## Other speech therapy rules still apply

Using telehealth does **not** remove the ordinary medical-necessity requirements for speech-language therapy. The service still has to satisfy the policy’s standard speech-language therapy criteria and documentation rules in **section 3.2.1.3**. For example, that section includes service-specific medical necessity standards for speech-language therapy, including documented findings for dysphagia-related treatment and other speech-language requirements.  
[[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), § 3.2.1.3, effective Feb. 1, 2025; current document confirmed]

## Bottom line

Speech therapy may be provided via telehealth under NC Medicaid **when telehealth is medically necessary for the beneficiary and is used appropriately as a supplement to in-person care**, not for provider convenience or productivity.

per_question.question: What medical loss ratio (MLR) must Medicaid managed care organizations meet under federal law, and how does NC implement this requirement?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under federal law, Medicaid managed care plans do **not automatically have to meet a nationwide fixed MLR floor unless the state chooses to require one by contract**. But if a state does impose a minimum MLR, the federal minimum floor must be **at least 85%**. North Carolina implements this through its prepaid health plan (PHP) contract by requiring annual MLR reporting under the federal method and by setting a **Department-defined minimum MLR threshold that is 88% in aggregate across all contracted PHPs**, with each PHP’s threshold calculated as a revenue-weighted average of rate-cell thresholds. If a PHP falls below its NC threshold, it must remit a rebate, make approved health-related contributions, or do a combination of both. [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438); [Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)

## Federal rule

### 1) What federal law requires
Federal Medicaid managed care rules require the state to ensure, through its contracts, that each MCO, PIHP, and PAHP **calculates and reports** an MLR under the methodology in **42 C.F.R. § 438.8**. But the regulation makes the **minimum threshold** conditional: **“If a State elects to mandate a minimum MLR,”** that minimum must be **equal to or higher than 85 percent**. So the federal baseline is:

- **Annual MLR calculation and reporting are required**; and
- **A mandatory minimum threshold is optional for the state**, but if imposed, it must be **at least 85%**. [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

### 2) How the federal MLR is calculated
Under **42 C.F.R. § 438.8**, the MLR is the ratio of:

- **Numerator**: incurred claims, expenditures for activities that improve health care quality, and fraud prevention activities; divided by
- **Denominator**: adjusted premium revenue, with taxes and licensing/regulatory fees treated under the rule’s denominator provisions.

The regulation also allows a **credibility adjustment** for partially credible plans. It specifies inclusions and deductions within incurred claims, such as provider payments, unpaid claim liabilities, certain withholds, and deductions like overpayment recoveries and prescription drug rebates. [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

### 3) Federal oversight when a state sets a minimum
If a state imposes a minimum MLR, **42 C.F.R. § 438.74** requires the state to report to CMS each plan’s:

- numerator,
- denominator,
- MLR percentage,
- member months, and
- any remittances owed.

If remittances are collected because a plan missed the state’s minimum MLR, the state must reimburse CMS for the **federal share** of that remittance and submit a methodology describing the state/federal split. [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

## North Carolina implementation

North Carolina’s PHP contract adopts the federal framework and adds a stricter state-specific threshold.

### 1) NC requires both a CMS-defined MLR and a Department-defined MLR
The NC PHP contract says the PHP must calculate and report aggregate MLR annually on two bases:

- the **CMS-defined MLR** under **42 C.F.R. § 438.8**; and
- a **Department-defined MLR** that is calculated similarly but with NC-specific adjustments. [Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)

For the **CMS-defined MLR**, NC tracks the federal method:
- numerator = incurred claims + quality-improvement expenditures + the lesser of fraud-reduction expenditures or fraud-reduction recoveries, as defined in **42 C.F.R. § 438.8(e)**;
- denominator = premium revenue minus taxes and licensing/regulatory fees, as defined in **42 C.F.R. § 438.8(f)**. [Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)

### 2) NC’s Department-defined adjustments
For the **Department-defined MLR**, NC permits some additions and exclusions beyond the federal formula. The contract says the numerator may include certain **voluntary contributions to health-related resources** that align with the Department’s Quality Strategy and meet stated conditions, such as meaningful local engagement and direct improvement of beneficiary outcomes. [Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)

The contract also excludes certain items from the numerator, including:
- certain required additional directed payments reimbursed separately by the Department,
- related-provider payments that violate payment limitations,
- interest or penalty payments for prompt-pay failures,
- prior-year rebate-related items, and
- non-claims costs, including PBM fees and spread pricing, marketing/branding, related-party administrative payments and margin, and administrative costs not allowed as health care quality improvement. [Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)

NC also requires:
- aggregation of data across Medicaid eligibility groups covered by the contract,
- a **credibility adjustment** for plans with **fewer than 380,000 member months** in the reporting year, using the federal credibility framework, and
- compliance with Department MLR templates/instructions. [Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)

### 3) NC’s minimum threshold
The NC contract states: **“The minimum MLR threshold in aggregate across all contracted PHPs shall be exactly eighty-eight percent (88%).”** It further says that each PHP’s own minimum threshold is calculated based on the PHP’s **capitation revenue mix**, using a **revenue-weighted average** of the relevant rate-cell thresholds. [Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)

So, compared with federal law:
- federal law permits a state-set minimum, but only requires that it be **no lower than 85%** if used;
- North Carolina uses that option and sets a stricter aggregate standard of **88%** for its contracted PHPs. [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438); [Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)

### 4) What happens if a PHP misses the NC threshold
If a PHP’s Department-defined MLR is below the minimum threshold, the contract requires the PHP to do one of the following:

- **remit a rebate** to the Department equal to the denominator times the gap between the threshold and the Department-defined MLR;
- **contribute to approved health-related resources** targeted to high-impact initiatives improving health outcomes and cost-effective care delivery; or
- use a **combination** of rebate and approved contributions. [Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)

## Bottom line

- **Federal law:** annual MLR calculation/reporting is required; a mandatory minimum MLR is optional for the state, but if imposed, it must be **at least 85%**. [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)
- **North Carolina:** requires PHPs to calculate the federal CMS-defined MLR and a state Department-defined MLR, and sets an aggregate minimum threshold of **88%** across contracted PHPs, with plan-specific thresholds based on revenue mix. [Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)

I checked the amendment status of both cited sources in the corpus; both were returned as the authoritative current documents for this question.

per_question.question: What are the specific criteria for NC Medicaid coverage of CAR-T cell therapy?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid covers CAR-T cell therapy when the beneficiary meets the general coverage requirements and these CAR-T-specific requirements:

- **The CAR-T product must be FDA-approved.**
- **It must be administered according to FDA-approved guidelines**, including:
  - indications and usage,
  - dosage and administration,
  - dosage forms and strengths, and
  - warnings and precautions.
- **It must be given at a certified or authorized treatment center.**
- **If the therapy is subject to an FDA-required REMS program,** the treatment center must be enrolled in that REMS program, and providers must be trained to manage:
  - cytokine release syndrome (CRS), and
  - neurologic toxicities.  
  [CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), § 3.2.1, effective 4/1/2025, current.

NC Medicaid also applies its **general medical-necessity/coverage standards**, meaning the service must be:

- individualized, specific, and consistent with the beneficiary’s symptoms or confirmed diagnosis;
- safely furnished, with no equally effective and more conservative or less costly treatment available statewide; and
- furnished in a manner not primarily for the convenience of the beneficiary, caretaker, or provider.  
  [CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), § 3.1, effective 4/1/2025, current.

## Situations the policy says are not covered
The CAR-T policy also specifically says Medicaid does **not** cover CAR-T therapy when, among other things:

- the therapy is **not FDA-approved**;
- it is being used **outside FDA guidelines** for indications/usage, dosage/administration, or dosage forms/strengths;
- a therapy that requires **REMS** is given at a facility **not enrolled** in that REMS program;
- the beneficiary is seeking **repeat treatment** after having previously received another CAR-T therapy;
- the beneficiary’s **psychosocial history** limits the ability to comply with pre- and post-infusion care; or
- current beneficiary or caretaker **noncompliance** makes adherence to the required medical regimen improbable.  
  [CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), § 4.2.1, effective 4/1/2025, current.

## If you mean prior-approval documentation
For prior approval, the policy calls for documentation including:

- a physician-signed **letter of medical necessity** documenting prior chemotherapy regimens and dates, clinical/social history, and indication for CAR-T;
- verification that the administering facility is a **qualified/authorized treatment center**;
- recent **HIV and hepatitis serologies**;
- diagnostic and procedure results, including **bone marrow biopsy** (not more than 6 months old); and
- a complete **psychological and social evaluation**, including compliance, support network, post-treatment care plan, and mental health/substance use/legal history.  
  [CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), § 5.2.2, effective 4/1/2025, current.

If you want, I can also give you this as a **short eligibility checklist** for case review or prior authorization.

per_question.question: Can an NC Innovations waiver participant request services that exceed their individual base budget, and what happens if they believe their needs cannot be met within the budget?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes. An NC Innovations participant may request services that cost more than the participant’s individual base budget if the participant believes their needs cannot be met within that budget. The policy says the SIS results and base budget are guidelines, not a binding cap on what may be requested or authorized; if the LME/MCO determines the services are medically necessary, they must be authorized regardless of the base budget. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment) (effective Nov. 1, 2016; current authoritative document per amendment check), “Category Assignment and Individual Budget Changes.”

If the participant believes the budget is inadequate, the policy indicates several things happen:

- **They can ask for services above the base budget.** The policy expressly allows a request for services “in excess of” the base budget when needs cannot be met within it. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment), “Category Assignment and Individual Budget Changes.”
- **Medical necessity controls.** The LME/MCO must decide whether the requested services are medically necessary; if so, the services are authorized even if they exceed the base budget. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment), “Category Assignment and Individual Budget Changes.”
- **If denied, the participant must be told why and how to appeal.** The policy states that if a request for authorization is denied, the LME/MCO will notify the individual of the reasons for the decision and how to appeal. It also references how to file a grievance regarding the base budget. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment), “Category Assignment and Individual Budget Changes.”
- **Supporting documentation may be needed for requests beyond the assigned budget tool.** The policy section on North Carolina Innovations lists materials that may support such a request, including updated evaluations, behavior support plan, medical records, and post-secondary services documentation when relevant. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment), “North Carolina Innovations.”

One related policy section also shows that when very high levels of support continue to be needed, the treatment team should review the person’s status and identify sustainable supports, including options within the waiver and outside it such as Medicaid State Plan services. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment), “NC Medicaid North Carolina Innovations.”

## Bottom line
The base budget is **not an absolute ceiling**. A participant can request more, and if the LME/MCO agrees the additional services are **medically necessary**, they should be authorized. If the request is denied, the participant should receive notice of the reason, appeal rights, and information about filing a grievance regarding the base budget.
